title: Memory Protection in Hardware
summary: Why 'user mode' isn't a polite convention — permission bits and privilege levels are checked by hardware on every single memory access.

slides.markdown:
Memory protection isn't a software policy that well-behaved programs happen to follow — it's enforced by hardware on **every single access**, using bits stored right in the page table and a hardware-tracked **privilege level** for the currently executing code.

A user-mode program physically cannot write to kernel memory or execute a non-executable page, no matter what the code tries to do — the check happens in silicon before the access is ever allowed to complete.

slides.subTitle: Protection bits in the PTE
slides.markdown:
Every page-table entry carries protection bits alongside its frame number: **readable**, **writable**, **executable**, and a **user/supervisor** bit marking whether user-mode code may access this page at all.

On every memory access, hardware checks the requested operation (read, write, or instruction fetch) against these bits for the target page — before the access is allowed to proceed. Any mismatch (writing to a read-only page, executing a non-executable page, user code touching a supervisor-only page) triggers a fault immediately.

slides.subTitle: Privilege levels / rings
slides.markdown:
Alongside per-page permissions, the CPU tracks a **privilege level** for whatever code is currently executing — commonly **user mode** and **supervisor (kernel) mode**, with some architectures (x86's "rings") offering finer gradations.

Switching from user mode to kernel mode isn't something a program can just decide to do — it happens only through tightly controlled hardware mechanisms (a syscall instruction, an interrupt, an exception), each of which hands control to a fixed, OS-defined entry point rather than letting arbitrary code jump straight into kernel privilege.

slides.subTitle: A protection violation
slides.markdown:
When an access violates the target page's permission bits or privilege requirement, hardware raises a fault immediately and traps into the OS instead of completing the access.

![A protection violation on a memory access triggering a fault that traps into the OS handler](assets/memory-protection-violation-fault.svg)

The faulting instruction never completes — the OS handler decides what happens next (usually killing the process with a segfault).

slides.subTitle: Segmentation's remnants
slides.markdown:
Before paging dominated, **segmentation** protected memory with base/limit pairs — an access was valid only within a segment's declared bounds. Some architectures (notably x86) still carry base/limit checks alongside paging, mostly for backward compatibility.

Segmentation alone struggled with external fragmentation (variable-size segments leave odd gaps) and doesn't compose as cleanly with the fixed-size-page abstraction the rest of the memory hierarchy is built around — why paging became dominant almost everywhere.

slides.subTitle: Paging-only vs segmentation+paging
slides.markdown:
| | Paging only | Segmentation + paging |
|---|---|---|
| Fragmentation | Internal only (last page per region) | External fragmentation possible at segment level |
| Complexity | Simpler — one mechanism | Two mechanisms layered together |
| Modern usage | Dominant (Linux, Windows, most ISAs) | Legacy remnants only (mostly x86 compatibility modes) |

Most systems dropped pure segmentation because paging alone gives clean, fixed-size protection units that compose well with everything else in the memory hierarchy, without segmentation's fragmentation headaches.

slides.subTitle: "User mode" is enforced, not assumed
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "User mode is just a software convention — well-written programs don't touch kernel memory."

**Why it's wrong:** if true, any buggy or malicious program could compromise the system by touching kernel memory directly. Protection must hold even against code actively trying to violate it — a convention alone can't guarantee that.

**Correct model:** privilege levels and permission bits are enforced by **hardware** on every access — user code is physically incapable of reaching supervisor-only pages. That's why protection is a real security boundary.
